hints: Use integration by parts with the logarithm as the factor to differentiate.
Take $u=\ln x$ and integrate $x^{-3/2}$ to obtain $v=-2x^{-1/2}$.
The remaining integral is another power integral; complete it before substituting the limits $1$ and $4$.
Use $\ln1=0$ and simplify the boundary terms to the required form.
walkthrough:
Apply integration by parts to $\displaystyle\int_1^4 x^{-\frac{3}{2}}\ln x\,\mathrm{d}x$ using the formula $\displaystyle\int u\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}\,\mathrm{d}x = uv - \int v\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}x}\,\mathrm{d}x$:
Let $u = \ln x$ and $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x} = x^{-\frac{3}{2}}$.

Assemble the integration by parts formula:
$$\int x^{-\frac{3}{2}}\ln x\,\mathrm{d}x = -2x^{-\frac{1}{2}}\ln x - \int (-2x^{-\frac{1}{2}})\left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right)\mathrm{d}x$$
$$= -2x^{-\frac{1}{2}}\ln x + 2\int x^{-\frac{3}{2}}\,\mathrm{d}x$$

Combine the terms to obtain the antiderivative:
$$-2x^{-\frac{1}{2}}\ln x - 4x^{-\frac{1}{2}} = -\dfrac{2\ln x + 4}{\sqrt{x}}$$

Apply the definite limits from $1$ to $4$:
$$\left[-2x^{-\frac{1}{2}}\ln x - 4x^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right]_1^4$$

Evaluate at the upper limit $x = 4$:
$$\text{At } x = 4: \quad -2(4)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\ln 4 - 4(4)^{-\frac{1}{2}} = -2\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\ln 4 - 4\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = -\ln 4 - 2$$

Evaluate at the lower limit $x = 1$:
$$\text{At } x = 1: \quad -2(1)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\ln 1 - 4(1)^{-\frac{1}{2}} = -2(1)(0) - 4(1) = -4$$

Subtract the lower limit value from the upper limit value:
$$(-\ln 4 - 2) - (-4) = -\ln 4 - 2 + 4 = 2 - \ln 4$$
This completes the proof as required.

ai_rubric.Integration by Parts: Integrates by parts and reaches $ax^{-1/2}\ln x+b\int x^{-1/2}\dfrac1x\,dx$. Completes the integration to derive $-2x^{-1/2}\ln x-4x^{-1/2}$, or equivalent. The final result is $2-\ln4$.
